source.title: Exploring the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in reasoning models

record.file_problem: The post text is present, but the cited Figures 2 and 3 are not included; their results are described qualitatively in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The post applies the original difference-in-means direction and weight-matrix ablation approach to newer models, and reports effects on refusal and harmless-task performance. It also tests ablation of multiple directions.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative refusal and MMLU outcomes, but not the figures' numerical values. The cosine similarities and ASR statements are included because the author presents them as experimental observations; cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The post applies Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means direction and weight orthogonalization to Qwen3 reasoning models. It reports that single-direction ablation is insufficient for larger models, while ablating several cluster-derived directions reduces refusal. This is a direct result arguing V1 needs restating (V4), tested in reasoning models (V8).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author concludes the refusal subspace is multi-dimensional also in newer reasoning models (Qwen3), with more directions needed for bigger models. They present a cheap clustering-plus-DIM method (with MINCOS selection) to extract multiple directions. Multi-direction ablation reduces refusal with little MMLU loss except in Qwen3 14B. The author explicitly says multi-dimensionality is not a new discovery.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means directions per harmful-content cluster and selects multiple candidates with MINCOS, rather than testing only one global direction. It follows the original weight-matrix orthogonalization approach, but does not ablate the embedding matrix or the first three layers.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect depends on the number of ablated directions and model size: a single direction is insufficient for Qwen3 8B and 14B, while multiple directions reduce refusal. Qwen3 14B is the stated MMLU exception; the author suggests its float16 editing, versus float32 for the others, may explain this. The post also says the two evaluators differ in strictness.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-direction weight ablation leaves MMLU (100 samples, 0-shot) not significantly degraded, except for Qwen3 14B, where float16 editing is suspected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablating several refusal directions preserves general capability comparably to single-direction ablation.

record.problems: The supplied post omits Figures 2 and 3, so the refusal and MMLU outcomes have no extractable numerical values. Harmless-task evaluation uses only 100 random 0-shot MMLU samples. Refusal is assessed with two LLM judges, and the post itself notes concerns about evaluator reliability. The author also acknowledges that the harmful-prompt dataset may lack diversity and could contribute to probe-direction divergence.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified values for individual ablation counts or model conditions are stated in the supplied text; the figure descriptions are retained as qualitative rows. No results cited from other studies are included.

untested.parts: Inducing refusal by adding the direction. Activation-level ablation across all positions. Capability under single-direction ablation.
Single-direction abliteration's capability cost. Complete refusal removal.
Whether jailbreaks suppress the direction. Training against ablation.
Affine vs. cone vs. dominant-plus-others distinctions. Probe/DIM SSR comparison is cited, not shown.
Separating the reasoning effect from model size. Non-Qwen reasoning models. Effects on reasoning traces vs. final answers.

missing.what: Per-cluster DIM directions from 74 HDBSCAN clusters yield about 12 non-collinear refusal directions with pairwise cosine around 0.3, which the author says are topic-interpretable.
missing.locator: Characterizing the refusal cone; Creation of the variety dataset

missing.what: From the author's SSR experiments, probe-based attacks beat DIM-based attacks (about 50% vs. 90% ASR); the models are not stated. This likely restates Winninger et al. 2025.
missing.locator: Computing the refusal direction through optimization yields better results

missing.what: Number of directions needed per model size and the judge-range compliance values in Figure 2 (figure not in text).

record.verdict_notes: Informal LessWrong post; figures are missing from the text, so all ablation outcomes are qualitative. Refusal is judged by two LLM judges (lenient Mistral NeMo, strict Gemini 2.5 Flash), on Q4_K_M-quantized models. The embedding matrix and first three layers are not ablated. Size and reasoning are confounded across the Qwen3 family. Several statements (the Llama 3.2 3B 0% ASR, and 50% vs. 90% ASR) are unsupported anecdotes or come from the author's prior paper.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test activation projection at every layer and position or adding the direction to induce refusals to harmless prompts. Harmless capability is assessed only on MMLU.
Does not establish complete refusal removal; the reported multi-direction result is a reduction in refusal.
Does not test training against ablation or robustness after such training. The reported evidence concerns direct direction ablation, not a separate jailbreak attack.
Does not establish whether the refusal representation is specifically affine, or compare all proposed geometrical descriptions.
No cross-language or cross-stage transfer test; testing different model sizes does not report transfer of a direction between models.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.
Although the experiments focus on reasoning models, the post does not test whether reasoning before answering changes the claimed single-direction mechanism.
